1:
Who wrote the psalm is unsettled, and Calvin lays out the options. One writer ascribes it to David at the second removal of the ark from Obededom's house, but the mention of David's name in the third person in the tenth verse tells against that. Others give it to Solomon, and Calvin quotes a judgement that the psalm is an exact epitome of Solomon's dedication prayer, its closing sentences identical with three verses here. Those who take the songs of degrees for pieces sung about the return from Babylon conclude instead that Ezra selected this ancient song for the second temple's dedication. Clarke reaches that position on his own: some attribute it to David without sufficient ground, others to Solomon with more likelihood, but most probably it belongs to the close of the captivity. Delitzsch also makes the speaker the post-Davidic church; Henry alone reads the whole as Solomon's address at his own dedication, pleading his father's vow.

What is to be remembered is disputed at the level of the word. Ellicott reports that the term rendered afflictions is the plural infinitive of a verb whose first sense is to declare, and prefers that: Lord, remember David and all his declarations. Delitzsch takes the verbal noun for all the care David had in procuring a worthy abode for the sanctuary, the verb meaning to harass oneself about something. Henry offers a wide and a narrow sense — all the troubles of his life, or his uneasiness that the ark was in curtains — and reports the rendering all his meekness. Gill leaves the speaker open: the prayer may be David's own, that God would remember his covenant, or Solomon's, that he would remember the promise that his son should build the house.

On the force of remembering they agree, and press it differently. Delitzsch defines the idiom: one remembers something to another when he requites what that man has done, or performs what he promised. Spurgeon presses the paradox of praying it at all — Jehovah changes not and will never forget a servant, yet for this very thing he is to be entreated. He notes the difference between this plea and a Christian's: David had no personal merit, the plea resting on the covenant graciously made with him. Henry draws the lesson forward: it is not amiss to put God in mind of our predecessors in profession, of their afflictions and of their prayers for those coming after. Calvin blocks one inference sharply: it is preposterous to argue from this passage that we may be benefited by the intercession of the dead, as if the faithful were calling an advocate from the tomb; they look to the covenant God made with David, which though given to one man was to be communicated to all.

The vow itself is read as hyperbole by all who comment on it. Gill says David does not mean he would never enter his house or sleep until the thing was done, but that he could take no quiet satisfaction until it was; Jewish commentators call the expressions hyperbolical. Clarke gives the resolve a practical shape: David would not pass another day before fixing on the ground and planning the building; and when told that Solomon should build the house, he still collected treasure and materials all the rest of his life. Gill and Clarke both remark that of this oath nothing is said elsewhere, while holding it was certainly made. Ellicott finds in the word tent either a reminiscence of nomadic times or an allusion to David's own wandering habits. On the name invoked, Clarke and Gill trace the Mighty One of Jacob to the patriarch's blessing, Clarke suggesting the heathen name for their stout ones may derive from it, and Gill recalling that Jacob was the first man on record to make a vow, and that it concerned the house of God.
6:
Ephratah and the fields of the wood must be identified before the verse means anything, and Ellicott admits the trouble. The verse has been pronounced inexplicable, he says, yet the intention is clear: what is heard and found can hardly be anything but the vow just quoted, since the feminine suffix on both verbs points back to the word he rendered declarations. That settled, there is no need to hunt for another locality, since Genesis, Ruth and Micah identify Ephratah with Bethlehem, and David's purpose would naturally be connected with his family's birthplace. The psalm still keeps close enough to history to recognise the discovery of the ark at Kirjath-jearim as a decisive step toward the temple.

Gill and Wesley take Ephratah for the tribe of Ephraim instead. Gill argues from the ark's having been at Shiloh and the Ephraimites being called Ephrathites, but observes that God chose not that tribe; Wesley adds that the city of woods is Kirjath-jearim, where the ark stood twenty years. Clarke takes both readings, the second the more interesting. On one construction the verse continues David's vow. But if the passage is taken as the captives' words in Babylon, he thinks the explanation plainer: we have heard that thy tabernacle was long at Shiloh in Ephraim, and afterwards at Kirjath-jearim, and then established in Jerusalem — but Jerusalem is now ruined, the temple destroyed, and thy people in captivity; arise, and re-establish thy dwelling in thy holy city.

Whether the next verse looks back or forward is disputed. Ellicott insists these words express a present determination rather than recall the past, the result of David's project being that this generation has a place of worship; and this holds even if the psalm belongs to post-exilic times, since a temple at any date could poetically be ascribed to David. He also prefers habitation to tabernacles, the same word being used in the fifth verse. Gill reads the plural spiritually, of the churches raised among the Gentiles, and reports the alternative that makes the clause an exhortation. Wesley identifies the footstool with the ark.

The petition that follows is recognised as a quotation. Gill notes that Solomon used these words at the dedication and closed his prayer with them, and takes the request for God to take up residence where he would have a stable rest, having walked in a tent since Israel came out of Egypt. Ellicott works the phrase ark of thy strength: it occurs nowhere else but in one other psalm, where strength alone denotes the ark, and the technical word for ark occurs nowhere else in the psalms. Spurgeon dwells on the name: the ark deserved it, since in captivity it smote its captors and broke their gods, and when brought back guarded its own honour by the death of those who treated it with disrespect.

The last petitions are read according to who is supposed to be praying. On the clothing of the priests Gill offers two candidates, the ministers of the word and all believers, who are priests to God and clothed with the robe of Christ's righteousness. He notes that where the words appear in Chronicles the reading is salvation rather than righteousness. On the closing plea Ellicott takes the obvious construction to be an intercession by the people for one of David's successors — in Chronicles it is Solomon praying for himself, whereas here he thinks of an Asmonean prince. He notes too that the expression to turn away the face of a suppliant, rather than to turn from him, is borrowed from court etiquette. Clarke and Wesley keep the anointed as the speaker himself, asking not to be cast out of God's presence. Gill refuses the merit reading: not for any virtues of David, but for the sake of the covenant made with him, and of the antitypical David in whose name prayers are presented.
11:
The oath is the hinge, and its force is pressed. Henry sets it against David's own: did David swear to find God a house? Then God swore to build David one, for he will be behind with none of his people. Spurgeon says we cannot urge anything with God equal to his own word and oath: he swears that our faith may have confidence, and cannot forswear himself. Gill meets an objection — no oath is mentioned where Nathan brought the promise — by appealing to the apostle, who is express that there was one. Ellicott renders the phrase not in truth but as a comment on the oath: it is a true oath, he will not depart from it.

What is conditional and what is not divides them at the next verse. Gill draws the line sharply: the first part of the promise is absolute and respects the Messiah, this part conditional and relating to David's seed, their observance of the law being the condition of the kingdom. He takes covenant and testimony for one thing, the law given to Israel as a covenant and testimony of God's will, in which the kings were to read continually and by which they were to rule. Clarke states the outcome: the condition was not kept and David's posterity were driven from the throne, but the true David reigns.

The choice of Zion is made emphatic by a list. Delitzsch runs through what Zion displaced — Shiloh rejected, the ark briefly at Bethel and Mizpah, twenty years at Kirjath-jearim, three months with Obed-Edom — against which Zion is the abiding dwelling-place; and the blessing that follows falls first on temporal need, then on the priests. Henry treats both choices as of divine appointment, and makes the promises about Zion's hill as applicable to the gospel church as those about David's seed are to Christ.

On the word for ever they go further than the verse. Gill argues that neither Mount Zion nor the temple can be meant, but the church, in whom God rests and abides for ever. Clarke makes the largest claim in the chapter: here the Christian church is indubitably meant, and after it there never will be another dispensation — Christianity closes all communications from heaven to earth, and man's nature is capable of nothing more excellent.

The blessings are then divided. On the provision Gill notes that the Hebrew doubles the verb — in blessing I will bless — taking it for certainty as much as abundance, and reports the rabbinic reading of the fertility of the land in time to come, when there will be no poor. Clarke finds the type of that abundance in the multiplication of the loaves. On the clothing of the priests Gill observes that more is promised than was prayed for, since salvation includes righteousness and every other blessing, and offers the same two candidates as before. Wesley reduces it to saving graces, Clarke to redemption through the blood of the Lamb.

The horn and the lamp close the psalm and are read messianically by all. Gill reports the Targum's rendering of the horn as a glorious King and the Jewish commentators who understand the Messiah; the budding he refers to the other name, the Branch. Ellicott makes the sprouting horn an image of vigorous life, its messianic application drawn out in Zechariah's song. On the lamp he prefers I have trimmed a lamp, the verb being that used of the sacred lights under Aaron's charge, combined with the promise that David should have a lamp always before God. Wesley takes the lamp for a successor to continue for ever in the family, and particularly for one eminent light. Clarke keeps it general — a posterity secured. On the last verse Gill divides the shame in time: Christ's enemies will be ashamed either here, in repentance, or hereafter at the resurrection.
